- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
We still "dial" phones that have no dials. We "hang up" calls with nothing to hang. We "roll down" car windows by pressing a button, and the save icon in most software is a floppy disk that many of its users have never held.

I love these fossils. Language keeps the shape of things long after the things are gone, the way a riverbed keeps the shape of water. Some are much older than the telephone. "Deadline" was reportedly a line around a Civil War prison camp that prisoners would be shot for crossing. A "clue" was originally a "clew," a ball of thread, the kind Theseus unspooled through the labyrinth so he could find his way back. Every detective following a clue is still, etymologically, holding a string in the dark.

What strikes me is that nobody decides to keep these words. There's no committee. They persist because they're useful, and usefulness doesn't require that anyone remember the origin. A word can do its job perfectly well while carrying a small, forgotten museum inside it.

It makes me wonder what we're fossilizing now. Maybe "scroll" will outlast screens, as it already outlasted actual scrolls. Maybe "footage" will still measure video centuries after anyone has measured film by the foot.

There's something comforting in it. The objects we make are fragile and get replaced quickly, but the words we made for them drift on, repurposed and unbothered. We don't so much discard the past as keep speaking it, usually without noticing.
---
